utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Good morning to you all. I'm afraid we still have to sit without Judge Parker today. So Judge Thelin and myself, pursuant to the Rules, will sit alone. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with one small matter before we start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It takes no time at all. With regard to the next witness, Grujic, he is not able to come next week. He can conclude his evidence this week, and then I believe it would have to go over, because of his professional commitments, until almost mid-June. So we have asked, but it is impossible for him next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to hear that, Mr. Moore. So, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to follow up on what Mr. Moore has just shared with us. I have some additional information in relation to Mr. Grujic, something that we find worrying, or may find worrying, but that depends on the Chamber's decision following what Mr. Moore has just said. I'm sure you know that we have received a great deal of documents, very comprehensive ones. Most of these documents we received last Friday. The following Monday afternoon more material was disclosed to us, which is the bulk of documents in relation to this witness, if I may say. These are documents in relation to Vukovar and nothing but Vukovar. And everything else that we have so far been receiving has mostly been in relation to Croatia as a whole and was about the both previous times he testified in the Milosevic and Martic trials. What we received two days ago is entirely new, entirely unfamiliar. It is only in relation to our indictment. It is to a great extent about Ovcara itself and about Vukovar, generally speaking, as well as the territorial extent of our indictment. Given the sheer bulk of documents that we received, I don't think we shall be in a position to cross-examine Grujic as soon as tomorrow. We would only like to ask you to take into account our position in view of the 48-hour dead-line. That is too little time for us to run all the checks that we deem necessary. The best thing for us might be that Mr. Grujic be examined in chief and then for cross-examination to proceed at some later date, once we have been given a chance to go through these documents that I say again are entirely new to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am not specifically dealing with this topic but I am obviously aware of what is occurring. I am a little surprised at my learned friend saying that he received documents on the Monday, because I am informed that in actual fact those documents had been delivered to the Defence on Friday but it was the ERN copies on Monday. The best way ahead, if I may submit, is for Mr. Smith to be contacted and perhaps at the next break for him to come down and deal with the matter more specifically, because he actually deals with that material. I have other areas that I have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On Monday we received batch 177; that was disclosed to us on the 29th of May. That's what we received, and this is the key document containing references to all of this. This is entirely new to us, and we received this on the 29th from the OTP. The afternoon of the 29th, if I may add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Well, I can see that there is a serious problem for the cross-examination. I suggest that we see where we get this week, and if it's impossible for the Defence to finish cross-examination then we will have to resort to the solution that Mr. Moore proposes, which is a bad solution, but which is inevitable, I'm afraid, if we can't properly finish the cross-examination this week. So we shall proceed with the evidence now. Witness, may I remind you of the affirmation you took yesterday, which still applies today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. May I just remind you of what we said yesterday about you making a short pause after each of my questions so that the interpretation may proceed smoothly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I'll try to keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, I would like to clarify something that we discussed yesterday briefly. You said you never did your regular military service because you decided to press on with university?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember testifying before this Tribunal in a different trial where you said that you never did your regular military service on account of eyesight-related problems that you suffered at that time. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'll read the relevant portion of the transcript from the Dokmanovic case. Page reference is 721, lines 10 through 13. "[In English] Very well. Did you see anybody wearing these five-point stars, did you serve the army, by the way? "A. No, because of my eyes."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember this, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that wasn't about me not doing my military service because my eyesight was poor. This was about poor eyesight on account of the fact that my glasses had just been shattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What was your prescription back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was minus 2.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On both your eyes, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was there anything else in addition to you being short-sighted? Were you suffering from any other illness of your eyes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You told us yesterday that the HQ of your unit was at Olajnica. Was this at a distance of about 200 or 300 metres from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I hope you will agree with me that this is a part of Vukovar which, with the exception of Borovo Naselje, had remained under the control of the Croatian forces for the longest time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Borovo Naselje, but I do know that the Croatian forces left Olajnica on the morning of the 20th. All resistance ceased and defence forces had been disbanded already on the -- I'm sorry, I've just made a mistake. Not on the 20th, but on the 19th. The morning of the 19th. All resistance ceased on the morning of the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any foreign mercenaries among your ranks who came to give you a hand with fighting the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet an HOS member named Jean-Michel Nicolier who was a sharpshooter in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met a French man who had been wounded. I met this man at hospital, but I had no clue he was an HOS member. People were saying that he was indeed a sharpshooter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about a person by the name of Zlatko Ovcar, also known as Deda, grandpa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he was perhaps an HOS member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: He was a member of your unit. What were his precise duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't in my unit, but he was often in the Olajnica area. I can't be more specific about his duties. I do know that he was an ethnic Croat, and I think he hailed from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have any indication that this man had taken part in the liquidation of Serbs in Vukovar's shelters and houses as combat operations were already under way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. There was no indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Upon your return to Croatia, did you ever meet this man and talk to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to university in Zagreb, and I once caught glimpse of him through the window of a passing tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you didn't talk to him, you just laid eyes on him, as it were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who Ivan Korac is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was another man who was at Olajnica at the time. I think he was from Vukovar originally. But he wasn't in the same group as me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was this person a member of the military police of the National Guards Corps, those were in charge of supervising the warehouse at Olajnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that he was a member of the National Guards Corps. I'm not sure if he was a military policeman though. I'm not sure what his task was, that he was supposed to keep an eye on the Olajnica warehouse. I do know that he spent a lot of time in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We talked about your direct superior yesterday, I'm not mentioning his name, but you know who I'm talking about, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to keeping an eye on the Olajnica warehouse, were he and your unit also not tasked with watching the Vukovar warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Vukovar Hospital, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't more than once or twice that we were told to go and secure the hospital courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In actual fact, you were standing guard there, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the exact time when you received these assignments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was sometime in late September.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said something about staying in the Olajnica shelter yesterday. Are you familiar with the fact that in October 1991 ZNG military police officers killed ethnic Serbs called Milko and Mirka [as interpreted] Orescanin, who were saying in this shelter. These people had previously resided in Otokara Kersovanija Street, number 59?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My next question may jog your memory. Do you know about this pub called Sid which used to be on Otokara Kersovanija Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Never heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did you know anything about a pub being blown up on Otokara Kersovanija Street at some point in July 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never, in fact, aware of a single pub on that street, not ever. The only catering establishment along that street that I knew of was the butcher's shop. That's all I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Throughout your time in the shelter at Olajnica and for as long as you were carrying out your assignments there, did you know of any ethnic Serbs being taken away from the shelter by any ZNG members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know that anyone was ever taken away, abducted, if you like, from the shelter, regardless of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were people being abducted or taken away from the nearby high-rise buildings, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your unit was supposed to provide logistics support to other units. You were supposed to look after civilians and the wounded and tracking down any spies, right? Fifth columnists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where were your supplies coming from, where did you get your logistical supplies from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean where did we get that from? Where was the base?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said your task was to get supplied, logistics; in other words, food, water, and other necessities. What I want to know is where were these goods kept before you eventually took them to other places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These goods were from Vukovar shops. The ones that had warehouses before the war. We were given permission to enter these warehouses and to distribute the food to civilians. In addition to that there were also clothes available. People fled from their homes with just small plastic bags; they had no change of clothing. The children didn't have diapers, so we found these supplies for them in warehouses of various department stores, shops and so on, upon receiving permission to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the food, given that Vukovar is in a hilly area and that there were many storage areas in town before the war where the food was stored, I suppose that this is what you used to provide these supplies for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand one of the words you used. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In Vukovar before the war broke out there were many underground storage areas where food was kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have in mind basements?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have in mind the large basements where the food was stored.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely there were basements where food was stored. But we didn't take food from those basements; we took it from warehouses of shops. Food shops. In addition to that, we went to silos on the Danube where flour was stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was food delivered also via the so-called corn road up until November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this corn road. The supplies that we used were located in various warehouses belonging to the shops in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that there were also other groups providing logistic support? One of them was located in the basement of the Vupik supermarket near the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the group for logistics which was active in the Hungarian school in a street --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that after the war, but I didn't know about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I can see that the interpreters didn't hear the name of the street. It was Radiceva Street. I suppose that you distributed food and water on a daily basis to these shelters that were in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost daily. And towards the end, as the shelling became more intense, perhaps we didn't distribute it on a daily basis at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume that you would turn over the supplies to the head of the shelter, who then would distribute it among the people in the shelter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you bring this -- these supplies also to the unit which was stationed in the palace of Count Eltz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps on one occasion we took some clothes to them. Perhaps we took some clothes to them once, or some food on one or two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, the distribution of supplies to the shelters would be conducted in such a way as to take the supplies to a centre, central area and then distributed further on on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Normally we would take it to the storage area that existed in each building. It was an area under the staircase where people normally kept their bicycles. We would put it there, and then from there on it would be distributed on a daily basis, as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, about one of the tasks your unit had, which was to care for the wounded. Can you describe it in detail, please, this care for the wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone was wounded in that area in Olajnica, wounded by shells, and later on by bullets, we would transport that person to the hospital. In addition to that, some people who were lightly wounded and for whom there was no more room at the hospital would be sent back and cared for, their wounds dressed, in the nuclear shelter, as needed. Also, if the hospital needed blood supplies, we would inquire about possible blood donors. On one such occasions my mother went to give blood, and she was then wounded. She was wounded in the area of her liver. In addition to that, the driver who took her to the hospital, on his way back, was wounded as well. Therefore, it was extremely dangerous to carry out any tasks, including the most humane ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me this: Given that you had these tasks to care for the wounded, did the command of your unit have a direct contact with the Crisis Staff which was located in the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what kind of contact you have in mind. We were in the hospital area almost daily. I don't think that there was any radio communication with the hospital Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear to me now, thank you. Let us now turn to the task of your unit pertaining to uncovering the fifth columnists or traitors. I assume you uncovered them or located them amongst civilians who were hiding in the shelters of buildings, residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We started having suspicions that there were people who were loyal to those attacking the town and shelling civilian targets. We started having these suspicions when there were occasions when water tanks -- water tank trucks would bring in water. Up until the -- mid-October, these trucks would bring in potable water. There were large numbers of civilians, and they would bring us water for food preparation and for drinking. Every time such a truck would arrive, a large number of people would gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. You told us about that yesterday. I'm interested in something else. It seems that you had suspicions about people being informants, and I would like to know about the procedure your unit applied regarding that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to describe that to you. So whenever a water tank truck arrived, within minutes very intense shelling would begin in the immediate vicinity of the water truck. We were on the look-out to see people peering through windows, and we could hear some soft firing sounds as though a small pistol was being fired, omitting some kind of a signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And then you would what, arrest these people and turn them over to the military police of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was simply trying to locate the area from which these shots were fired. Other people who were not part of my group tried to locate more closely these people. I think they were then detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the high-rises near the shelter in Olajnica elderly people were arrested, allegedly in possession of radio transmitters and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, possible. If it was related to what we discussed previously. I personally never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The fifth columnists, the informants who were arrested, were they ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After being detained, do you know where they were taken and questioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were taken to the command headquarters, and as to what happened to them there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you say the command headquarters, do you have in mind the nuclear shelter under the municipal building in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether they were taken there or to the military police, which was in the building next to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fate of the people taken into custody and detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Up until the 15th or 16th of November, 1991, you were hoping that the Croatian leadership would send military assistance to Vukovar, as requested by Mile Dedakovic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only military assistance, but also civilian aid. Water, food and reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And it was only after the 15th or the 16th of November that you realised that the help wasn't going to arrive, and it was then that you became aware that Vukovar would fall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was very young at the time, I didn't have an abundance of information about the situation as a whole, and this is what I knew at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And on the evening of the 18th November 1991, you took off your uniform and the insignia of the ZNG, you threw away the membership card of the HDZ, you took off your rosaries and that -- your valuables, and then you decided to go to the hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything is correct except for the membership card of the HDZ. I never belonged to any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, why did you do that on the evening of the 18th? Did somebody tell you to change into civilian clothing and go to the hospital on the following day? Did perhaps your commander tell you this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was already at the hospital at that time, that he wasn't in the Olajnica region at all. We heard, I don't know from whom, that all resistance was to be discontinued and that it would be smart to discard all of these belongings. As for the decision to go to the hospital, it wasn't made until the 19th in the morning when the lady came wrapped in a white flag, the one that we described yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 18th in the evening, did other members of your unit who hadn't decided to leave Vukovar also take off their uniforms and discard their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your commander, the one we mentioned earlier, was somebody trusted by Dr. Vesna Bosanac. He was in constant communication with her, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was due to the nature of our tasks. As the time went by, I'm now referring to late October and November, we were also tasked with providing some of the food supplies to the hospital. The bread was baked at Olajnica and delivered daily to the hospital for the wounded. Also, whenever possible, we took other food supplies to the hospital. So the commander was in constant contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he ever tell you that it was actually Dr. Bosanac who informed him that the defenders of Vukovar should come to the hospital in civilian clothing so that they could leave Vukovar in convoys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you decided to go to the hospital in civilian clothes, you certainly expected the International Red Cross or some other international organisation to peacefully evacuate you and your fellow fighters to Croatia. That's what you told the Canadian officers; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard that unfortunately your mother was wounded, and that at one time you went to visit her, I assume in your uniform and with your weapons, when you were not on duty, and that this happened on an almost daily basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But I did not have a uniform except for yellow boots, which were civilian boots. And I did not carry weapons into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you mention those yellow boots, was there anything written on them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I can remember. Those were yellow boots produced by the Borovo factory for export. They were civilian boots, but they were very high quality and very comfortable, which is why we were given them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You don't remember that the shipment that was issued to you was stamped with the words "Defenders of Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the boots I received certainly did not have the words "Defenders of Vukovar" stamped on them. As to whether there were any letters on them or not, there may have been a logo or a trademark name of foreign origin. I cannot be certain about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 18th of November in the evening when you took off all the things you mentioned, were you already aware that the commanders of the Vukovar defence had already left Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that information was going around at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You didn't leave Vukovar, as you told us yesterday, because of your mother, and because you hoped, as you told us today, that you would be peacefully evacuated by some international organisation. Was another reason for your not attempting to leave Vukovar the problem of minefields, which were laid by various groups of defenders in various parts of town, and you were not sure where precisely they were, so it was risky to move along those routes. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that there was great fear of leaving the town on one's own initiative. Both because of the minefields, as well as the forces, the hostile forces, the JNA forces and others surrounding the town, and there was also fear of being involved in a direct fight with them, being taken prisoner. So I did not dare go along those routes. I knew that Vinkovci was the closest free area, and that was over 12 kilometres away through the fields. It was a very dangerous and uncertain route to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On your arrival in the hospital on the 19th of November, which you have already described, and during that night you saw many of your fellow fighters in the hospitals. They were in civilian clothes and, like you, they wanted to leave with the hospital convoy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Some of them put on plaster-casts and bandages to make it appear that they were patients of the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were wounded, and they had bandages, but there were also others who were not wounded and put bandages on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Others put on white coats so it would appear they were hospital staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You then saw a soldier, Damjan Samardzic, whom you mentioned here, who was wearing a white hospital coat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Maybe not on the 19th but on the 20th, but I did see him wearing a white coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You did not put on a white coat because you thought you would be included in the convoy as your mother's escort; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't want to put on a white coat at all. And yes, I did think I would be accompanying a wounded person; that is, my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I now wish to move to that part of your statement which concerns your arrival in the barracks and my friends -- my colleagues will deal with the rest. I would like to go back to what you said about some people leaving the bus and entering another bus, and that they received some blows as they were passing by. When you spoke about this beating, you said it wasn't very serious. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were slaps and kicks in the bottom, or in the stomach. As for their seriousness, it was less serious than what happened later on to the other people in the hangar at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at Ovcara, you told us yesterday that you were met by a gauntlet of Chetniks and that there were more of them in the hangar. Outside there were some 10 of them, and some 15 inside. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that after passing through the gauntlet --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 10 on each side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: -- you said they took your money and your jackets. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see Exhibit 256, photograph 22, please. Thank you. Can we zoom into the hangar we are discussing in the centre? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you see this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you show us the hangar in which you were detained? Excuse me, could the usher hand you a pen so that we can all see this in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this hangar here. [Marks]. This is where we came in, this is where the gauntlet was. This is the direction from which the buses arrived. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please mark this hangar with the number 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Put number 1 there and circle it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you mark the place where the gauntlet was with 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to indicate the place where your belongings were taken, your jackets and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, at the entrance, and they threw them here. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to mark that with 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this photograph will be Exhibit 527.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will not need this photograph any longer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that your glasses were broken right after you entered the hangar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After your glasses were broken, bearing in mind the situation you described in the hangar, you described it yesterday, and the fact that you are short-sighted, and quite badly, would you agree with me that by the light entering the hangar only from windows which were high up, you couldn't really distinguish or discern details in the hangar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also light coming in through the door, not just through the windows, which were high up. But it's true that my perception was diminished and that as I was unable to see details. I was, however, able to see the overall situation very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that in view of the fact that you are short-sighted you could only see what was happening close to you, but you couldn't see what was happening further away. I'm referring to your observation of detail.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that at one point a person made a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it might be better to move into private session at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were asked by my learned friend yesterday about those sounds of heavy machines. One seemed to be nearby, and the other seemed to be at some distance. Would you agree with me if I told you that you never mentioned this to the OTP investigators who took your statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did mention this at some point, I can't remember which specific statement that was. But I'm sure I did mention the sounds of heavy machinery working nearby. The sound spread far and wide. I am positive that I mentioned this somewhere. I'm just not sure about which statement. Maybe the questions were not sufficiently specific for me to answer in some other statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, one thing I can tell you is that you never mentioned this in any of your numerous statements, the numerous statements that you gave upon your return to Croatia, or those that were taken by OTP investigators or, for that matter, during your evidence in the Dokmanovic case, or during your evidence to the investigating magistrates in Zagreb, Osijek and Belgrade. The only time you ever mentioned this was in the Dokmanovic case. But what you said was quite different. You said you heard sounds of heavy machines at work somewhere in the distance, which is quite different, I'm sure you will agree, from what you told us yesterday and a while ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a matter of distance, right? I did say at some point that I had heard heavy machines at work. I did say that. So much for that. One thing that is open is the distance, the actual distance of these machines. When I arrived outside the hangar the sound seemed to be coming from the right, this sound of heavy machinery operating. The distance is definitely open to debate. It certainly wasn't that nearby, because if it been I would have seen the machines. I'm not sure where they were exactly. They may as well been somewhere behind the building, somewhere I couldn't see them. But one thing is certain: I did hear these sounds of heavy machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: These heavy machines sound, this was a sound that might have been produced by a self-propelled machine-gun or by a tank or by another piece of machinery that wasn't exactly light?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It might have been excavators, for example, or loaders, tanks. Any piece of machinery with a powerful engine. It's very difficult to distinguish these different sounds, and that's why I wasn't particularly specific when I said heavy machinery. It's a very general description.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please just explain why you failed to mention this in any of your statements to the OTP or in your evidence before the Osijek and Belgrade courts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me one thing: Did anybody ever ask that specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think you were asked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, so that may be the reason I never gave the reference. When I was actually prompted, I did say so with no hesitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But do you remember that perhaps in the Dokmanovic trial you weren't asked this specific question, and yet -- the page reference is 711, line 25, and 722, lines 1 through 4. That's the reference. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember being asked. I do remember saying that somewhere. You say this was in the Dokmanovic trial. If there is a transcript that shows that I said this, then that is probably the case. But I can't remember whether I was actually prompted on that occasion or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Over the last 15 years, which is the period covered by the various statements that you gave, did you ever talk to members of the special department of Croatia's government for proofing witnesses who are bound to testify before the Tribunal in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk to anyone from Croatia about this Tribunal. No one ever accosted me on behalf of Croatia as a state over anything to do with this court. I only ever talked to personnel of this court, investigators as a matter of fact. People who introduced themselves as employees of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss your testimony here with other persons who gave evidence about Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the best thing for us might be to take our break now and then be back so as I can start my examination. But if you think the best thing to do would be to start now, I might as well do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. My name is Borivoje Borovic on behalf of Miroslav Radic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You testified in chief yesterday that in your neighbourhood there were houses inhabited by civilians and civilians only during the JNA attack, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: However, you also stated yesterday that control of your neighbourhood shifted. At times it was JNA-controlled, and at times it was ZNG-controlled, the paramilitary unit known as the ZNG; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that at certain points in time you were stuck, as it were, between the JNA units on the one hand and the ZNG units, the paramilitary units on the other, caught in a cross-fire, as it were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time, from the 24th of August until the 15th of September, this entails 22 days, I never left basement during that period of time. Therefore, I can't tell you whether my house was ever caught in the cross-fire between these two forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how do you know that at a certain point in time your neighbourhood was under the control of one forces and later on the forces on the other side, those belonging to paramilitary formations? How did you know about that then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in front of my house, in the street there was a check-point with sandbags belonging to Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that in front of your house and further down the street there ran a defence line of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally there was a line positioned in Otokara Kersovanija Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question. We learned here that in the water-tower there was a cache of weapons. I'm asking you whether you know that there were sniper nests in the water-tower belonging to the paramilitary ZNG forces and, if so, during what period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's just take it fact by fact. I never heard that there was a cache of weapons in the water-tower. Second, I never heard that snipers were positioned in the water-tower. And third, these formations in town were not paramilitary formations but rather those of ZNG, the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this means [as interpreted] that in your view the ZNG was a regular Croatian army with regular uniforms, insignia and with legally procured weapons or not? Or was perhaps everything illegal and paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the ZNG was a regular army of the Croatian state. Just a minute, let me complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please let me complete. The uniforms were different. The town was encircled for two or three months. People couldn't change into different uniforms, and as the weather grew colder they started wearing civilian clothes. As for the origin of weapons, I am not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You say that you didn't have a uniform. Can you please explain it to me how come in a regular army you did not have a uniform, and you were a member of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just explained to you that it wasn't possible to have the uniforms delivered to us. There was no access into town. There was no way a truck could have delivered shirts to us. The bird couldn't fly into town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us conclude with this: If you were indeed a member of the regular army, were you properly trained? Were you prepared to be a member of the regular Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't prepared and trained, but I wasn't involved in military operations either. I was involved in taking care of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. You went to the Vukovar Hospital. Do you know which ZNG unit acted or was active in the hospital compound at the time when you went there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which unit was positioned on the roof of the hospital and opened fire from there when you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no one on the roof of the hospital, because the upper storeys were extremely unsafe. The hospital was constantly shelled, targeted from the planes. You know the occasion when a large bomb, this so-called Krmaca fell on the hospital. There was absolutely no one on the upper storeys of the hospital. It was senseless, there was no point in putting anyone on the roof because the hospital building wasn't high enough to gain any advantage from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you go to the hospital on the first -- for the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September. This is where -- when I donated blood, and I think that I spent a night standing guard in the hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some kind of a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in accordance with all Geneva Conventions firing from hunting weapons is banned because it inflicts very serious suffering and bodily injury?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with Geneva Conventions. I suppose that serious and grave injuries can be inflicted with hunting rifles, and I myself never fired from one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. And before we break, please tell us this: Which nuclear shelters in the hands of the ZNG did you know about at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the nuclear shelter at Olajnica -- or, rather, that shelter was not taken by the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any Serbian military formations there, or just the ZNG units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several members of the ZNG inside the shelter itself. However, when in shelter, they were unarmed. In one building entrance there were 400 to 500 civilians. Those civilians were of all ethnic backgrounds, and in that nuclear shelter there were no Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the nuclear shelter in Borovo Komerc and do you know under whose control it was, under control of which forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that shelter, but I can't tell you anything about it because I'm not really familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Did you hear that that nuclear shelter was also under the control of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that perhaps some 10 years later in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear that the nuclear shelter at the hospital where you as a member of the ZNG stood guard was also under the control of the ZNG and the Vukovar MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, the nuclear shelter at the hospital was not under control of any army or the MUP or the ZNG. It was a civilian and medical facility; it was not under anyone's control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who stood guard at the hospital? Members of which formations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the ZNG. But they did not guard the nuclear shelter itself, just the outside perimeter of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this nuclear shelter located inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's in the basement of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, was there any nuclear shelter under the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about under the ZNG headquarters, was there a nuclear shelter there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one there. I think that that was the former military department office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And -- thank you. And it was under the control of the ZNG, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- that is the shelter that was under the control of the army and MUP, and I believe that there were no civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. How many people could fit into the Olajnica shelter where you had your ZNG base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, about 400 people. Towards the end, as people from Olajnica started leaving buildings on fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you how many people could fit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally over 500 people would cram inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In your previous statements the figure you mentioned was 700, but that's all right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said 700, that pertained to the hospital. When I came there on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. And my definitely final question. Was there a large shelter where there were civilians, ZNG and MUP members in the Vupik basements? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the Vupik restaurant, across from the Eltz palace there was a nuclear shelter -- no, I apologise, not a nuclear shelter, rather that was an old wine cellar. And there were only civilians there. I know about that because we took some food to them several times, and water. I didn't see any ZNG members there or MUP members either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And finally can we agree that all nuclear shelters and all larger shelters during war operations in Vukovar were under the control of the ZNG and MUP of Vukovar and not, as you call them, Serbian forces? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness has given a series of answers to specific questions. And all my learned friend is trying to do is to structure a question in a way that circumvents the earlier answers. And I would submit it's an unfair question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fail to understand what my learned friend Moore was trying to say. The witness gave very firm answers to all questions. I'm not trying to avoid any topic. I think that this question was a completely fair one. Since this man took part in logistical support and since he toured all of these shelters, and that's by his own account, all I'm trying to do is to reach a conclusion that would be helpful to the Trial Chamber in establishing what the situation was in all the large shelters in Vukovar. So I'm asking that the witness be directed to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. But I don't recollect the witness saying that the shelters were under the control of the ZNG and the MUP. So I think you're taking it further than what the witness actually said. That's my understanding, but you may wish to clear it up. But we have to have a break soon, so can you clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly will. I suggest for us to take a break now. Thank you. If you think that it's time for the break. I had just one more question remaining regarding this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I think for the sake of the tapes that we need to have the break now. So we will resume just before half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic. Before you start, Mr. Borovic, may I ask you to think of the pace of your questioning because the interpreters have been struggling with this. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In all larger nuclear shelters that we have mentioned so far, did you ever see in any of them members of these so-called Serbian forces or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the shelters I mentioned previously, I didn't see members of the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I think that we have clarified this and we can move on. Did you say to the Trial Chamber who was in command of the ZNG forces in Olajnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the commander of my group, but there were some other members of the ZNG there who would come there to rest. They were members of other units of the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Marin Mercep was the commander of your group. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who was in command of your group then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we discussed this in private session. I don't know if I am allowed to say this now, publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Marin Mercep somebody in charge of the group with which you tried to break through out of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Marin Mercep was in charge of the group with which I wanted to, I intended to leave. However, I never departed with them to attempt to break through from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did your group engage in any combat during these Vukovar events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My group was not active in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us who directed the civilians to go from the nuclear shelter in Olajnica to the hospital in an organised fashion? Was that done by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the woman in a white flag arrived, the civilians split. They formed groups going to the direction of the hospital and the market. I assisted them in finding the route from the shelter in Olajnica to the hospital, because the situation was a very difficult one. There were children, six, seven and eight years old, and even some younger ones, and they had emerged into daylight after three months of darkness. They were terrified. In the vicinity, one could still hear shooting and occasional explosion. In the crowd of civilians, including women, children and the elderly, I was one of the very few males. As I was accustomed to moving via the routes which were not frequented by civilians between Olajnica and the hospital, I helped these civilians in finding the proper road to reach the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you to give answers that are brief, because we have to cover a lot of material. My question was: Did you lead the column on their way from Olajnica to hospital? You could have just answered with a simple yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to be as clear as possible, so I'm giving the answers that I find appropriate. Whatever time it takes, no matter how long it takes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I think that I am in charge of this cross-examination, so you will have to follow my cues. When asked by Mr. Vasic, you said that you dug parts of your uniform, your weapons and rosaries into ground before going to the hospital. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was afraid. I was afraid of them finding these items on me personally. I had no use of weapons any longer. And as for rosaries, they were an evidence of me being a Croat. As for the uniforms and the boots, that was yet another thing that could have given me away as a member of Croatian forces. So I went from Olajnica to the hospital as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When asked by Mr. Vasic, you also said that the ZNG members put on fake bandages or plaster on parts of their bodies which were not injured, hoping to appear as the wounded. You also said something similar to the investigators. And when asked by Canadian investigators earlier and today by Mr. Vasic, you said that some members of the ZNG put on white coats hoping to pass themselves off as hospital staff. My question, once again, is why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is that all this was done out of fear. We were afraid we would be punished as members of the ZNG, which had offered armed resistance to the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did someone attempt to surrender with weapons after the 18th, to the best of your knowledge? Someone who was a member of the ZNG? Did they hand in their weapons, put their hands up and say, "I am a prisoner of war," thereby acquiring all the privileges pursuant to the conventions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such case in the area I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that Marin Mercep was a member of a special ZNG group laying minefields in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible he was a member of that group, but I don't think minefields were laid inside the town, only outside the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Are you guessing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm guessing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived in the hospital, on page 3 of both the B/C/S and the English versions, you said that in the evening of the 19th of November nothing was happening in the hospital, and that you slept on a chair until the morning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead. You have them before you. This is your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, page 3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me the date of the statement, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The only statement you gave to the OTP, and it's on page 3. I will tell you the date. It's the 19th of June, 1995. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And do you confirm today that that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At what time did you reach the barracks coming from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what time it was precisely. It was certainly in the morning hours, before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told my colleague that you spent at least two hours at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So if you spent three hours in the barracks and that you left Ovcara when dark fell in a van, that would mean that you spent at least three to four hours at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose one can check meteorologically when dark fell on the 20th of November, and you can work out the precise time of my departure from Ovcara. It's very difficult for me to pin-point the time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was simply calculating. You told us at what time you were separated off in the hospital, then you went to the barracks, you say you spent three hours there, and finally yesterday you said that it grew dark at around 1700 hours, that's 5.00 p.m., in November. And this would mean that the time was three to four hours. However, that's not so important. My question is the following: During the time you were at Ovcara, did you see anyone taken outside in front of the hangar and killed on the spot? Did such things happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were there, did you see some group separated off and taken to be shot or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long were you there standing in front of the hangar before you went towards Velepromet by van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Across from the entrance-way to the hangar, during the time you spent there, and you said you set out when it was dusk, which means that you could still see for a while, did you notice across from the gate to the hangar, across the road from there, a big hole in which there were corpses? Did you see that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday answering Mr. Moore's question you described the first person to arrive in the hospital on the 20th of November. You described his appearance, his uniform, but you didn't tell us his age. The first person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the first person who entered the hospital and told us to go outside? My assumption was that he was around 50, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. After this in your statement to the Prosecutor, and yesterday answering my colleague's question, you said in great detail that after they lined up, as you said, Major Sljivancanin arrived, accompanied by another officer whom he addressed as Captain Radic, and when he said that he should search the people you were asked by my learned friend, Mr. Moore, that he said more than once, Captain Radic, search the people; Captain Radic, search the people; Captain Radic, search the people. That's what's on the record. You also stated that Sljivancanin and Radic did not issue orders to the members of the Territorial Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you did say that this captain issued orders to his own men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did you notice whether the people receiving orders had white belts on, like the ones worn by members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you remember then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the men to whom orders were issued were wearing olive-drab uniforms of the JNA, that they were youngish, and I would say they were conscripts. They searched us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We heard that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to tell us whether during the time you spent in the hospital, before you left the compound, you noticed soldiers with white belts anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw one with a white belt, but he was from Vukovar. And he was older. He wasn't a conscript, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was this man from Vukovar with a white belt on his uniform doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. He was just standing there talking to some people. He was threatening some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: He didn't participate in the search?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't participate in the search.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to have Exhibit 170 shown on the screen. That's page 3, please. Could the usher please give the witness a pen?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this photograph on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is this a photograph of the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you now indicate the place from which you observed what we have just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark this with 1 and circle it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the place where Mr. Sljivancanin was standing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around here. Shall I put 2 and circle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And where was the captain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Right next to him. Mark it with 3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to tender this into evidence, this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 528, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that this captain was about 180 centimetres tall, that he had a moustache and a solid-colour military uniform, and that he had a Bordeaux-coloured beret on his head, a dark red one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And you also said he entered the bus with a list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we heard from you that you made a great many statements, that in 1992 you made a statement to Lavoslav Bosanac, the husband of Vesna Bosanac. We did not understand in what context and where the statement is, as it has not been delivered to the Defence. What we do have, however, is your statement to the Canadian investigators which you made in March 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Mr. Lavoslav Bosanac, I did make a statement to him, but he did not write it down. It is not documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I am now asking you about your statement to the Canadian investigators in March 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was around that time, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid wasting time, I see you have all these statements in the file before you. Then you made a statement to the Croatian authorities in Osijek some three months later; that is, in December 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Then to the centre for gathering documentation about the Homeland War in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: To the OTP in 1995 and before a court in Zagreb in 1996 and 2004. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You stated, among other things, before the centre in Zagreb for gathering documentation about the Homeland War in 1994 in paragraph 1, page 2 of English, of the English version --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I look?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. It's on page 2, paragraph 4 in B/C/S. You told us that the captain was a security officer, and you said before the court in Zagreb that he was aged between 35 and 40. On the 27th of March, 2006 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On page 9 on Rule 61 you said that he was wearing a dark red jacket [as interpreted]. My first question is: How do you know that he was a security officer? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an error in the transcript. Instead of leather jacket, it says dark red jacket. I read leather jacket. Now colleague Moore is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no objection to the question; it's a perfectly reasonable question. But what has preceded it has been reference to a number of statements. In my submission, the witness should have an opportunity at least of having access to those statements and his attention directed to them. Because the way it is now, it's very difficult to follow for anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: That's a fair comment, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, but there is a follow-up. I simply listed these statements for the witness to confirm, but before I go into details I wish to have some footage played. It is very brief. And I would like to ask the witness to look at it. It concerns the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is this an exhibit or another document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is footage delivered by the OTP to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give you the number. It's V000-0625-1-A. So this is something in the possession of the OTP, but it has not been tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to my learned friend for that assistance, but would he be kind enough just to remember perhaps to serve on the Prosecution if he is going to be cross-examining on any document or exhibit -- or indeed video, that we could have some notice of it. I thought the understanding was 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I respect my learned friend's suggestion, but this has not been done by the OTP so far. We have had footage, and this is the first time I've heard that I have to deliver in advance something in the possession of the OTP. It's not a problem, but it has not been the practice so far. By your leave, I would like to proceed. If this is to become the practice, in accordance with Your Honours' ruling, I will certainly comply with it. We would be very happy if what the Prosecutor wanted to show to the witness would be delivered to the Defence 48 hours before the precise footage that is to be shown. May I play it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can stop it right there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This is a JNA officer. Do you recognise the environment shown in this footage? Is this, in fact, outside the hospital on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be the 20th, but could be the 19th too. I didn't approach the hospital from that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that there were wounded JNA members in the hospital too, since you seem to have been to the hospital a number of times.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this perhaps as much as 10 years later in Zagreb. I have heard about this, but I didn't witness this myself when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about this person in the previous footage armed, wearing a beret and a moustache?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have a full screen shot, please? Stop right there and zoom in, if you can, or do a full screen view of the image? Thank you. Thank you, this is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am certain that I'm not, in fact, able to identify this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What led you to believe that the captain you have been mentioning was a security officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I get the transcript, please, if the usher could give me a hand with this. And if I could please have a look at the document you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You have the statement right in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I free to have a look?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: By all means. It is the centre for gathering documents on the Homeland War, the date is the 6th of July, 1994, paragraph 1, page 2. The English reference is page 2, paragraph 4. It's just a single sentence. I didn't make any copies for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the Croatian in front of me, and can I just have a minute to find this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Page 2, paragraph 1. That's your reference, sir. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I've got it. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You want me to read that portion out to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what it says, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does the statement not indicate that Captain Radic, who was in charge of that list, went from bus to bus and that he was some sort of a security officer there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. But the time reference here is to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
