utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was some sort of -- their security officer. The sentence implies that this is an assumption on my part. It is not a fact that I am stating with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What does this mean to you, be a security officer, security. What does that word imply?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the Court don't have a copy of it, and my translation does not say he was "a security officer." The translation I have was "he was their security guard." And there is a big difference in relation to that, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In both B/C/S versions the gist appears to be the same, that this was their security officer. If the English reads "their guard," I can accept that, I can live with that, as long as this is confirmed for us by the witness himself. It might be that one of these versions is simply erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a captain who acted as a guard or was Captain Radic, in fact, a security officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see the whole statement was based on some accounts. You can see in terms of the time-line that I was already in some sort of a row here, and a little later I'm talking about what happened at the barracks. So I would not really be very adamant about this sentence as providing a definition. It's in more general terms that I'm discussing this situation. He came there, he read out names from that list, and those people were eventually returned. They were sent back to the hospital. That's what I'm saying here. I didn't know this at the time. There are certain inaccuracies in this statement. Inaccuracies about things that I said at the time, but not based on my own experience. It was actually later on that I learned that those people had been sent back to the hospital, which was, in fact, true, but which I didn't know at the time. When I give evidence before a court, I normally get specific questions and I try to provide specific answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As their security, I'm quoting you, what exactly did you mean by that, regardless of any possible interpretation? Did you imply that he was a member of the Security Service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't implying that. I was implying providing security right there. I wasn't implying that he was a member of any service or anything. I am unfamiliar with any military services.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And secondly, what about your statement on the 27th of March, 1996? Have you got that? The OTP can follow, I'm sure. This is page 9. You said the captain was wearing a leather jacket. Do you remember that, sir? Do you remember stating that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said the interpretation was erroneous because it wasn't a dark red jacket, it was a leather jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify this, Witness. It's not a poor translation, the statement that I'm showing you. It was the interpretation that I was receiving a while ago. In this Rule 61 statement, you were quite specific, you said Captain Radic was wearing a leather jacket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine, but I do need to go back to that statement. If I could please have a copy made available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Again, we do have a copy. The statement was given on the 27th of March, 1996.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in my set of documents. Can I please be allowed to receive a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This one is in English. Can you use that or not? I'll give you a copy anyway. There you go. Even a glancing look will easily reveal to you that the reference there is to a leather jacket.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that it was a leather jacket. It's possible that there was some confusion about the colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just to keep this straight, can we please have this placed on the ELMO. Therefore, everybody can see for themselves that the reference here is to a leather jacket as being worn by that person. This is the fourth sentence down the page. It's a very brief answer. Number 3. I've had this shown to the OTP and to the Chamber. My question: "Was he wearing a monochrome military uniform or, in fact, a dark red beret? Which is true? You stated all these things, which is true?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the barracks and the bus, I still see his face, his appearance in my mind clearly. I was under the impression that this was a leather jacket, but I may, in fact, have been talking about the colour here. It may have been a leather jacket, but then maybe not. If we're talking about when this person got on the bus, then it must be the same person, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I was asking you about the jacket, not about the person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leather was maroon, dark brown, verging on grey and greenish.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that he was not wearing one of those monochrome military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This jacket may as well have been part of a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see anyone else outside the hospital wearing a uniform consisting of a leather jacket, the top and the bottoms a different item of clothing? Did you perhaps notice anyone else within the hospital compound wearing an attire as motley as this and still a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not within the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the hospital compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not within the hospital compound either. It was -- it wasn't before the next day that I actually clapped eyes on a person wearing that sort of clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We shall no longer be requiring this on our screens. We have established that there were a large number of persons on the bus outside the hospital, many of whom have testified before this Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber is familiar with their names, is privy to their names. I will comply with our established practice and will not be giving you the names of all these witnesses who testified to the same circumstances as our present witness. I will be using transcript reference numbers to point you in the right direction. There is a particular witness who testified before this Court. The reference for the Chamber and the OTP is page 5279, line 21. The transcript date is the 1st of March, 2006. The statement -- or the evidence reads as follows: "Once we had been searched, I heard Major Sljivancanin say that we should all get on the buses. It was an order that he issued." The question was: "Who was the order issued to?" And the witness answered: "A man who didn't appear to have a rank and must have been aged about 40." As for the situation in the barracks after the hospital, on 5459, line 6, the question was: "Do you remember anyone getting on the bus and calling their names out?" And the witness answers: "Not as far as I remember. No one read any names out. There were no lists there. Nothing." This is a witness who appears to have been on the same bus as you. It's a fact which is still to be tried by the Trial Chamber. The next reference is 6330, line 7, the transcript date is the 20th of March, 2006: "Q. There were these two men you say were in charge of the entire operation of searching the people there and of separating them off. Do you know who these two men were? Do you know their names? "A. No idea." Page 6335, line 1, further down, the same witness says in relation to the barracks: "Two soldiers got on the bus, one of them was carrying a list from which he read out names. I can't remember whether any of the people inside my bus were taken off. I did notice, however, that people from the other buses were, in fact, taken off. Those two soldiers, can you describe which group they might have belonged to?" And then the witness answers: "The JNA. They were JNA men." So this other witness mentioned no officers, just two soldiers, not a word about an officer wearing a leather jacket. If indeed there had been one, he certainly could not have been identified as a member of the JNA; this is at least what the Defence claims. On 3240, line 4, dated the 25th of January, 2006, that's the next reference, the witness says: "Yes, at the time this JNA major was in charge of the entire operation. Everything that happened was being supervised by him and was done pursuant to his orders." Further down the page the witness explains that this was Major Sljivancanin. On page -- I won't be quoting the whole page for you, since that's not necessary for you at all. On 3240, line 20, the question reads:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this -- this was at one of the hearings where a lot of things weren't clear, even the Presiding Judge Parker stepped in to make sure that everything was clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So then we have the following dialogue on that page: "Q. Did you see any other JNA officer wearing a uniform at the time? "A. At the time, I did not see any other JNA officer. However, it was later on that I found out from the detainees who were in the camp with me that there had been another officer within the hospital compound. He was a lieutenant and he was involved in the searches conducted by the soldiers and in escorting people to the buses." The same witness, on page 3248, lines 4 through 20, stated as follows. The question was: "Q. You mentioned that officer who got on the bus. I think you used the word 'lieutenant.' Who was that lieutenant? Was he familiar from before? "A. I don't know who the man was. I couldn't get a proper look at him. He stood at the front door of the bus. He was the officer who was in charge of lining people up, of searching people, and physically taking prisoners to the buses. "Q. Can I try to clarify this situation, just to avoid any misunderstanding. You say that you found a major there, you found out his name was Major Sljivancanin, as well as this lieutenant. But that was earlier at the hospital, whereas here you mention a lieutenant as being on that bus. What everybody would dearly like to know is whether this lieutenant you saw on the bus was the same as the one you had previously seen at the hospital. Can you perhaps help us with that? "A. Yes. "Q. Well -- So I think this was Mr. Moore's question, if I remember correctly. "A. It was the same man." And now, Witness, in addition to these three witnesses there are another three, a total of six witnesses in relation to the bus, P-009, P-012, and another witness who I believe you have referred to yourself; I'm not repeating his name here. Not outside the hospital, not outside the buses, not in the barracks, not one of them ever heard that there was another captain, Captain Radic, standing next to Major Sljivancanin. Nor did anyone hear anyone else calling out for Captain Radic to go and search you and yet you were together in all these different places. All right. Having confronted you with all of this, my question to you is: Do you stand by your previous statement, or is there perhaps a trace of uncertainty now? Are you perhaps now no longer sure that this person was Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sljivancanin was addressing the man standing next to him as Captain Radic. He did this more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So you abide by what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: As you abide by this claim, I have submitted this statement to Your Honours, pages 13 and 14, I have also delivered it to the OTP. It is a statement made in March 1993. Excuse me, I don't think these have been handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We haven't got any document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moore, do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's the Canadian document, and I can return it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although the witness does have this document, and we have established that the Court has it also, would you please find -- this is the first statement officially made by the witness, and it refers to the following. The witness says: "On the 20th of November" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please give me the page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I said pages 13 and 14. On the 20th of November, 1991, in the morning, as you stated on page 13, first they took out some people on the list and so on and so forth. And then you said the following, and I think you underlined it. (redacted) "Then an order was issued by a JNA officer over there. I don't know what his rank or name was. That all men should go outside. He lined us up there in rows. We were searched twice in detail. We were searched by two younger soldiers, which means they were conscripts doing their regular military service. Sljivancanin was coordinating this." So you said he was coordinating it and another one was issuing the order for the search. You said that you did not know the rank or the name of the officer who issued that order. That's what you told the Canadian investigators. My question is the following: Why did you not then say what you told the Court in great detail yesterday? Why did you not help those investigators establish who this other officer was and he is very important? You only said that you do not know his name or his rank, and it was only six months later, making a statement in Croatia, that you said this was Captain Radic, and then you went on repeating this, and this exacerbates his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What do you say about the statement which you made then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement was made, and you can see there are parts here which are inaudible, and on page 13 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Leave aside the inaudible parts. I have been very clear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be very clear if you did not interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be allowed to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It's a fair comment, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was did he mention Captain Radic anywhere in that statement, or did he, when a precise question was put to him, say that he did not know the name or the rank of the person participating those activities, whereas later on he identified him as Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic's name is not mentioned anywhere in this statement, but there is no direct question either asking me whether I knew the name of the person issuing the order. I was not faced with that question, which is why I did not reply to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's your response. In that same statement when you said, and you confirmed this today, that a bus with husbands and relatives of the medical staff was released, as you learned later nowhere in the statement to the Canadian investigators or here do you mention Captain Radic in connection with the barracks. Can we agree that this is not there in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it is time for lunch and to give the interpreters a rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic [sic]. We will now have a lunch break that will last until a quarter to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I see Mr. Smith on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon. This is just a brief scheduling matter. I received some information this morning in relation to the next witness and the Defence's concerns about their ability to cross-examine him this week. Just to clarify one matter, in relation to the material that was disclosed to the Defence, the Prosecution admits that some very significant material was disclosed to the Defence on Friday and that was addressed with Judge Parker in Chambers; and then on Monday one further document, which was a list in relation to 16 people; and then on Tuesday a map was disclosed, just a very simple map. But as far as the issue of whether or not the bulk of material was disclosed by the Prosecution on Monday or whether it was disclosed on Friday, I've spoken with my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, and it's quite clear, and he's had a re-look at his disclosed materials, and I think he accepts that the material, the bulk of the material was, in fact, disclosed on the Friday. The meeting with Judge Parker was on the basis that if the Defence had any issues or problems with cross-examining this accused -- sorry, this witness in relation to the new material, that we could clarify that. And as a result of that meeting, as you know, this witness and the next witness were swapped in the order of appearance to give the Defence more time to prepare for cross-examination. The Prosecution are prepared to proceed with the next witness. However, the Prosecution's concern is if cross-examination is delayed until a later date because, even as of this date they say that they are not in a position to cross-examine him on the new material, we would ask that the examination and the cross-examination be kept together, because the material, in fact, was new to the Prosecution as much as it was to the Defence. We only received that on Friday. However, we only received notice today that the Defence perhaps would like further time to cross-examine. We assumed that the witness would be heard this week. The witness has some pressing issues back in Croatia. So if, in fact, the cross-examination was put off, we would ask that they be put off together, because he kindly accepted to be -- to being placed out of order last week as a result of what had happened. But the Defence have one particular issue, I think, in relation to the basis of the charts and tables that were presented to the Defence and would be led in court, and perhaps they will explain more clearly that they would like the underlying documentation in relation to do that. The underlying documentation in relation to people killed, missing, detained, expelled in relation to Mr. Grujic's report, would be enormous. Absolutely enormous. And the question is there needs to be a compromise, I would submit, between presenting the picture through the statistics by this witness and only having relevant documentation provided to the Defence. But perhaps the Defence may be able to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the first matter of principle is this: The Defence does not wish for any postponement in the trial, and up to now we were prepared on many points to cross-examine this witness. You now find yourselves in the situation where you do not know what the position of the parties is. Perhaps I'm going to take a bit of your time, but I think it's important. We have had excellent cooperation with Mr. Smith so far concerning problems and various solutions to problems. The main portion of material arrived on Friday. We received it on Monday with ERN numbers, but what concerns us is what arrived on Friday. When we had a meeting with Judge Parker, in that meeting we told him that at that point in time we didn't know anything about the material. We had no information concerning it except for what Mr. Smith told us just before the meeting. What is truly worrying for us is that we want to find an efficient solution. As for Mr. Grujic, two weeks ago we received material which was related to his main expertise and his testimony in the Milosevic trial, then in the Martic case, and we also received some charts. What we received on Friday and several days prior to that, I think on the 22nd and 26th, and this is something that Mr. Smith can confirm for you, places the expert report of Mr. Grujic in a situation where it becomes of crucial importance, because Mr. Grujic has now started analysing the status of persons, their position, and he embarked on a completely new analysis concerning the persons who were moved from the area of Vukovar. And this is the material that we received on Friday. He now submits to us the results which were compiled by his office, and these results are truly important. So far in our cross-examination you have an able to see what they pertain to. So we have only the results, but we do not have sources based on which these results were based. This now relates to a certain period of time. We spoke to Mr. Smith, and we said that this would open Pandora's box if we now asked for thousands and thousands of pages to be delivered to us. We do not wish this. We wish to find a compromise. And as a result of that we suggested for the examination-in-chief of Mr. Grujic to commence, even perhaps the cross-examination to commence. However, we will be unable to get a lot of answers, and that in turn would open Pandora's box. Mr. Smith can confirm this to you. We have received charts so far where Mr. Grujic put in the number of civilians, the number of defenders, the number of refugees. So we have these results, but we cannot verify the sources for these results. And this is what concerns us right now. My colleagues and I discussed this at length. We are prepared to have Mr. Grujic start testifying, but there is this problem that we thought it was our duty to inform you about if we embark on a detailed analysis of his testimony. So, once again, we are prepared to have this witness come into the courtroom, but in the last few days completely new material was delivered to us, and this is something that Mr. Smith can confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, may I ask you what was agreed upon with Judge Parker was about the bulk of the documents except for those, the witness statement and the map that were you given yesterday. So at that moment in time your estimate was that you were going to be able to cross-examine within the two days that are available this week. Is that correct? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had a very constructive, albeit abstract conversation with Judge Parker. At that point in time when we were talking to him, we didn't know what was to be disclosed to us that afternoon. We did not receive that material until after the conversation. Once we received it, we informed Mr. Smith and Judge Parker that this new material pertained to the persons who were from the indictment but were found in different graves, which was a new and significant fact. As for the information submitted to us, as Mr. Grujic's lists that pertain to his final results for those who were killed, expelled, detained, and so on, from the municipality of Vukovar, at the time, at the relevant time I had no such information available to me. We discussed only 15 persons. That was what we discussed with Judge Parker. And we agreed to have a change in the scheduling of witnesses at that time. However, now, after we have been able to study this material, we now fear that a lot of new questions can emerge from this, and I would like for Mr. Smith to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Smith. But in the time you have had so far -- let me put it differently. You are sort of, in terms of a compromise, waving the possibility to see the whole set of underlying set of materials, so what you were then going to do anyway, if we would have cross-examination next week, was to base yourself on the material that you have now in your -- at your disposal, and you are saying that this is something you can't do by Friday, basically, that's the problem. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No, I do confirm Mr. Lukic's point that the material that was given to the Defence on Friday was very significant in relation to the case, and they hadn't received that material before that. We handed it to the Defence as soon as we received it. In relation to the material they received on Monday, it wasn't a witness statement, it was a list of 15 names in relation to one grave site. If the Defence had happy to commence cross-examination of this witness immediately after the examination-in-chief, if that's what I believe Mr. Lukic had said, the Prosecution would be quite obviously prepared to start. As far as underlying material being provided by the Prosecution to the Defence, in previous cases of this type, because the amount of underlying material can be so great in relation to statistics of this type, sometimes it's just unreasonable in terms of resources to be able to do that. Maybe a compromise could be that if the cross-examination -- they hear the evidence in chief, if the cross-examination commences, and then subject to that cross-examination Your Honours might either determine whether it would be appropriate for underlying material to be provided to the Defence or not. Because it could become an endless exercise in that -- to that degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Is there a reason, Mr. Smith, why we have received this material only now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The material -- there is, in the sense that when the expert report was filed with the court, it was an expert report that was used in the Milosevic case and the Martic case that related to Croatia more generally. As a result of scheduling of the witness, the expert report was reviewed, and it was realised it was deficient in terms of the material in relation to Eastern Slavonia in this case. So, in that sense, there is a lateness on the Prosecution in that regard, but as soon as we received it we handed it to the Defence. And one thing we might add, is the witness, I think it's been discussed already, cannot attend court next week. He would have to come back -- he can come back on the 12th. But we're happy to start the examination-in-chief, if the cross-examination would follow immediately after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber has to reconcile the interests of a fair trial with the need of an expedient trial as well in the interests of justice. So I think it's in everyone's best interests that we continue with the examination-in-chief. I see, Mr. Smith, that the time that you have scheduled is four hours. If perhaps you could try to reduce a little bit on that time, and the Defence could, from its side, try to organise themselves in the very efficient manner that they have been organising themselves so far, maybe we could try to see where we get on Friday. And if it doesn't work, then we will reconsider the issue and decide accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I will do. I will start cutting my questions now, Your Honours. Would Mr. Grujic be starting first thing tomorrow morning or would you expect him to be starting this afternoon, just to be able to advise him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: If possible, this at afternoon, but that obviously depends on the rest of the cross-examination. So Mr. Borovic, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let me just remember where we left it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: A question for the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... do you think that you may, you and Mr. Lukic, finish the cross-examination in such a way this afternoon that we can stall call upon the witness or, in the alternative, that we have to schedule him for tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is yes, as far as I'm concerned. I don't know about Mr. Lukic. I don't know how long he will take. I believe that we will conclude today, because I won't take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that my cross-examination will take an hour and 15 minutes. Could be less, but to be on the cautious side I would say what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Well, it seems, Mr. Smith, that we won't be able to call the witness. So let's schedule him for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In the documents disclosed by the OTP to the Defence there are two documents, one of which I provided to the Chamber but with two ERN numbers, which are 0357-1712, and the other one is 0357-7958. As regards this document, I would like to put several questions to the witness, but prior to that I would like to establish what he knows from these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My first question is: Do you know Igor Kacic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Emil Cakalic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I'm afraid the Chamber is not with you. Those documents, what are you referring to? Is this the last, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I submitted it to the registry, to the Chamber. That's the second document. In this set of documents there are two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry for interrupting you, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I almost started criticising my colleague here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question to the witness: Do you know Kemo, the Albanian who was the member of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kemal Saiti. I used to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about Zvonko Vulic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was his nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Salas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Professor Ivo Matic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I submitted the English version to the Chamber, so you should have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This statement that the usher just gave you has all of these names, and these are allegedly the names that you provided to the person who wrote the statement together with you. So I wanted to check whether you were the source of information for these names, because that's what it says in the heading. And I would like for you to confirm it. And based on that, Your Honours, I am now putting to the witness this document, and I will ask him to read out the fourth line of this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the hospital compound they put them into buses, into six buses. Officer Sljivancanin was present there. He later became a general. And there was another officer Simic there? Not sure that that was his name."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see that in this official note you say that in the -- you say the hospital and then the barracks, and then you mention the person who was taken out of the barracks, but nowhere do you mention Captain Radic. You only mention Officer Sljivancanin, this is beyond dispute, and Officer Simic. So if I were to tell you that it is the position of the Defence that the commander of the military police company Simic was the one who secured the hospital on the 20th, together with the military police company, and that they were the ones frisking you, would you then, in this third attempt, perhaps start doubting your statement about Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask about that. Just leave this be for the time being.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but may I answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to be clearer to begin with so as not to confuse you. Regardless of the fact that there is no date on the face of this document, regardless of the fact that the only name being mentioned there is your name, this is an official note that the OTP has served on the Defence. Fortunately for us there is information indicated here which you provided. The officer who was right there in addition to Sljivancanin was Officer Simic, rather than Captain Radic. What I'm telling you is that on the 20th of November, and there will be a lot of Defence witnesses to corroborate this, Simic was an officer of the military police company. Is this clear enough? That is the position of Captain Radic's Defence. Would that affect your testimony that the person you saw there was Captain Radic then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that Officer Simic was there, but that does not in any way affect the heart of this matter. Because Sljivancanin was addressing the man standing next to him as Captain Radic. I heard that loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My next question. You said you didn't do your regular military service with the JNA, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Although you didn't serve your term with the JNA, do you know that officers are only addressed by using their ranks but never their names? That's what all the rules say. If it really had been the case what you have told the Court, Captain Radic, do this or do that, it would follow logically from your statement for Captain Radic to say, I understand comrade, Major Sljivancanin, which would never, possibly not even then, be the case in the JNA. There's one reason for you. Another reason. A while ago, and this is evidence too, you drew Sljivancanin and Radic, their respective positions, as standing next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect to my learned friend, I have no objection to questions being asked on the relevant material but it's not a case for my learned friend to give either explanations or attempt to give evidence in relation to the issue. In my submission, that's what he's trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. All I'm trying to do is be as fair as possible in telling the witness that certain circumstances are just not possible. We shall have our own military experts testifying to that. I'm just trying to show that there could have been no such communication. On the other hand, we have had a photograph admitted into evidence showing Sljivancanin and Radic standing next to each other side by side, as the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question: Would there be any reason for someone who is standing next to you to be addressed five times in a row as Captain Radic, Captain Radic, Captain Radic? He wasn't calling to him over a great distance. The man was standing right there, let's face it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how officers address one another in the JNA. I'm entirely unfamiliar with that. As for the first part of your question. Secondly, I'm only telling you what I saw while I was there, what I heard. Sljivancanin addressed the man standing next to him as Captain Radic. I'm not sure if that's by the book or not. I know that this was the case. He said this a couple of times. He repeated this just because there were quite a number of people that needed frisking. I suppose that was the reason why he addressed Captain Radic several times, not just once.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going back to the fact that none of these witnesses who might have had reason to blame Captain Radic never said they'd seen him anywhere near the buses or in the hospital. But let me just refer again to your statement, what you said the first time around during your evidence to a Croatian court in a statement that I've quoted from, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the Croatian authorities, Croatian police, or anyone from the Croatian judiciary ever show you any photographs of the men that stand accused here before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you think there is a possibility that they may have shown you photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anyone in Croatia has ever shown me any photographs of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps some other people or officials did show you photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it was actually officials of this Tribunal who showed me the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You mean the OTP, not necessarily the Tribunal as a whole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the OTP. I mean their investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just one photograph or several?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please be kind enough to say how many and just whose photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps as many as two photographs of Captain Radic and one or two photographs of Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not go into the technical aspects of this situation, but when the investigators showed you these two photographs, you know what the rules are in the whole wide world for situations like these when someone is being formally identified via a photograph. They should have shown you quite a number of different photographs, including a photograph of the accused. It's some sort of a line-up, and we all know how that is done by the book. There have to be a lot of different faces and you have to pick one. Is this how they did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did show me a great number of photographs, all sorts of photographs, and then once I have ID-ed the accused, they showed me some photographs of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you identified Captain Radic, the accused, how exactly did this work? Did they place on the table in front of you a large number of different photographs showing different people, asking you to pick out Captain Radic or did they just show you his photograph asking you to identify him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they only showed me his photograph, but this occurred 10 years ago, so my memory of the event may not be perfectly accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Perfectly accurate in relation to what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they showed me this 10 years ago, I can no longer quite remember if there was just one photograph being shown or several.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps -- are you inclined to believe that there was just one or are you inclined to believe that there were several?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on at a later stage there was just one, but I can't say what the case was originally, whether there was one or many being shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honours. I'm not pressing this further. When was this one photograph being shown to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this one time that I was interviewed where this one photograph was being shown, and then perhaps several different photographs were shown at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Whose photographs, these other photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After several different photographs were shown, then individual photographs were shown, and those were photographs showing Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who else was depicted in these photographs that you were shown in addition to Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People whose faces meant nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to what happened in Vukovar and the accused, the only photographs that you were shown were photographs of Captain Radic, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: These other photographs that you have mentioned, you are starting to modify your initial answer, and I am sorry, I don't think I can possibly give up on this now. You say there might have been several different photographs being shown of several people, and you say the faces were unfamiliar. What did these people look like; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what these other people looked like. They do appear to me to have been wearing uniforms in those photographs, but I couldn't possibly be more specific about what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. At any stage during your evidence did members of the security and intelligence service of the Croatian state take part, the SIS or the HIS people, Croatian intelligence service, at any stage during your proofing for your testimony here or during the time when the indictment was still in the pipeline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At no time was I approached by anyone like that, or at least the people that did approach me did not introduce themselves me in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If these people did not introduce themselves in this way, who was it that you worked with while being proofed for your testimony here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not prepared by anyone for my testimony here. None of the official Croatian bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we now please go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise once again for not stating this right away. But here is our position. On the 20th, in the hospital, Captain Radic did not take part in any selection process, in any issuing of orders to frisk the person entering buses. Captain Miroslav Radic did not write any lists, nor was he at any point in time in the barracks in Vukovar, especially not on the 20th of November, 1991. At the time Captain Miroslav Radic was 29 and not 35 to 40, as you described in some statements. Captain Miroslav Radic is not 180 centimetres tall, but rather 192 centimetres. Captain Miroslav Radic never had a dark red beret, and he always wore a uniform. He never ever wore the leather jacket, which is perhaps a minor detail. This means that we challenge your evidence in its -- in all of its portions. You were a member of the ZNG, and you were influenced by the Croatian media and Croatian organs, and you invented what you said here. The film that I asked you about called "100 Days of Vukovar," which was adduced into evidence here, depicts an officer with a helmet and moustache uttering the words, "Vukovar must fall tonight." The Croatian media, for years, while showing that movie, stated that that was Captain Radic. All of these are manipulations and you fell victim to them too. This person on the footage is not Captain Radic but another person, and all of this is known to the Trial Chamber because we provided the name of that person to the Trial Chamber when adducing evidence. So I am telling you now that it was only Captain Simic who could have been in front of the hospital doing things that you described. This means that you either malevolently or by virtue of being in error did what you did to implicate the accused, and you did that by providing this information. That's all I have to say to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I am Momcilo Bulatovic, one of the Defence counsel of Veselin Sljivancanin. On behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence team, I will be putting questions to you now. I will do my best not to repeat the questions put previously by my friends, unless I need to clarify something for my own benefit. I would like to ask you to wait before answering my questions so that we do not compromise your identity and protective measures.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As you were answering the questions of Mr. Borovic you mentioned some photographs which were shown to you by investigators and so on. A statement was written, was drafted by The Hague investigators on the 19th of June, 1995. Please tell me: Was a note compiled or a statement about photographs being shown to you? And, if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many photographs were shown to you? You said a large number. Do you remember from what period of time these photographs were? Were they photographs of uniformed men, civilian and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were several photographs of men in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were those individual or group photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether any video footage was shown to you as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that any video footage was shown to me. If you are now referring to the 19th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely the date that I was interested in. As I see that you keep referring to the 19th of June, 1995, questioning whether that's what I have in mind, and knowing that Mr. Borovic put questions to you as to whether you were prepped for testimony by SIS and HIS, you said that no, you were not prepared in any way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But the way you phrased it could indicate that you were perhaps prepped for some other testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some video footage was shown to me when I came here in 1998. It was shown to me by officials of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what case it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You testified before courts in Croatia in two cases. One was the case versus Veljko Kadijevic in the cantonal court in Zagreb; and the other one was in the Osijek court in the case against Vuletic, Ivica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Before testifying there in these cases, did you have any discussions with any members of any Croatian bodies, organs, and was any material shown to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never talked to any Croatian officials, not while preparing to testify, and not in relation to these events. Before these two instances when I testified, I never talked to anyone, either Croatian representatives or any international official, so I didn't talk to anyone. I received notice to appear to testify, and as provided by the Croatian law, I went to court to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to any media representatives before or after your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one? Which testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Any of your testimonies and any of the instances where you gave statements. Both statements given to the OTP investigators in the Dokmanovic case, when you gave statements to the commission for detained persons, and when you testified in Osijek, in Zagreb, and when you were interviewed by the judge from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only time was in 1993. And that was a statement I gave to the ITN, a British media outlet, and also a portion was given to the HTV, Croatian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was the reason for you giving statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The British officials contacted me first. They wanted to establish the truth; that was back in 1993. Nothing was known about those people. And these men came to me with some information and they said that in order to put the whole process into action, to establish the truth, was for me to testify. You know, what the journalists normally tell you. And it was then that I gave a statement. I think that the gentleman who interviewed me was called Terry Lloyd. And after this was made public, I was invited by the HTV to come to a programme called Slikom na Sliku where the host was Mr. Kopljar and that was the only media appearance. The reason for that was that I wanted to have the truth established about what happened to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you: In 1993, and we all know that the events at Ovcara occurred in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you keep silent for two years and wait for some sort of ITN to turn up with some sort of information instead of approaching some Croatian or international services to report what you knew about Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first statement was made immediately after I arrived in Croatia. It was made to Mr. Lavoslav Bosanac. As far as I know, he did not record it, and that happened right after I arrived in Croatia. So I did not wait for two years. I immediately spoke out. And you asked me about the media, this was my first and only testimony in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to this statement that you made to Lavoslav Bosanac, which was not recorded. How did you come into contact with him? Did you call him, did he call you, did anyone mediate in this, why did you go to see him of all people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Zagreb in order to put some documents in order. I think I wanted to report my arrival to the Vukovar club in Zagreb, and there I heard that the government office for displaced persons was in Zagreb. It was located in a street called Brace Oreski, which is now called Republike Austrije. And I asked who was employed there, and there was some journalist there, Mr. Estereiher, and Mrs. Vukovic, and Mr. Lavoslav Bosanac was also there. I knew him as the husband of Dr. Vesna Bosanac. In this capacity, I thought that he was a suitable person for me to tell the truth to, and he was very surprised at this. That was the first time, as far as I know, that people on the Croatian side heard about Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion when you made that statement to him did you write it down in your own hand, or was it just a conversation, an internal one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just an internal conversation, and then he told me to go to the medical headquarters of the Croatian army, which was in the Maksimir area in Zagreb, and there I made a fuller statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "fuller," does that imply that it was recorded somehow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was written down or whether there were any transcripts. I did not sign anything to the best of my recollection, and I wouldn't know whether the statement was recorded or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When speaking to Lavoslav Bosanac and in this medical headquarters in Maksimir, were you alone with the person taking the statement, Mr. Bosanac, in the former case, and I don't know who in the latter, or were more people present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of Mr. Bosanac it was just the two of us; whereas, in Maksimir there were several people. The only person I recall is Dr. Juraj Njavro. There were some other people there, but I don't remember who.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you mention Dr. Juraj Njavro, what was he doing at the time? Did he have a post or an office in the Croatian government at the time you made the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this, but you can check it. It was in February 1992. One can check what he was doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. But I knew his face from Vukovar. He was a doctor from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him in Vukovar Hospital at the time you went there in the way you described before the 19th and throughout the time you visited the hospital from the 15th of September onwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him once or twice in passing within the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in your departure on the 15th of September. You say you went to Olajnica. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about 500 metres as the crow flies, and 700 metres maybe by road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know anyone at Olajnica when you went to report there, which would mean you had information as to where the headquarters was, or did you go to that shelter and then find there was a staff there and then report? How did your reporting to the defenders of Vukovar happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came there with my mother, we settled in. And there were a few armed people there. They were defenders and they started keeping guard. I immediately reported saying I wanted to stand guard too. And, when necessary, I volunteered to go to fetch food or water or clothing. We can't really call it a proper headquarters in the nuclear shelter or in Olajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have omitted to mention something. I asked the witness something on page 91, line 7, and it might reveal the identity of the witness, because it mentions the place where he resided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: So let's play it on the safe side and redact it, although I'm not sure it's really necessary, but to play it on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you join a unit right away and did that unit belong to some kind of military formation at Olajnica or in Vukovar in general?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day or two later I joined my unit in which I remained until the end, and it was part of the 204th Vukovar Brigade of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in command of the 204th Brigade, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile Dedakovic was the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We have heard here that you had parts of a uniform, so I would like to know with what you were issued when you joined the unit. We heard something about boots, but did you get any other gear or equipment and, if so, what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning I was not issued with any uniform parts. About a month later I received boots, some caps or hats. We couldn't really call that a uniform. And weapons were issued at night for the needs of the guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were you issued with any insignia of the Croatian army and, if so, what insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not issued with any insignia of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In the unit where you were, were there fighters who had uniforms and insignia and, if so, can you describe what kind of uniforms and insignia these were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the commander had a uniform. It was a complete uniform, and his insignia were a chequer-board emblem on his cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few of those who had caps would sometimes put the chequer-board coat of arms on them, and a few others had parts of uniforms. We, as a logistics unit, were not issued with uniforms because uniforms were scarce.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Answering a question by my colleague, Mr. Vasic, you described how you went to the hospital on the 19th, and you say that the evening before that you took off all your insignia, everything that had to do with the guard, that you discarded your papers, your rosaries and everything else. So what I want to know is how many people removed their chequer-board insignia, how many people destroyed those papers, how many people threw away those rosaries and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was five or six from that group and a few others from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "from outside," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who happened to be in Olajnica, and they were not members of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What group were they members of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of the Croatian army, the 24th Brigade, but not that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were all the weapons and all those other things buried in one place or different places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of only one place. In the sand behind the nuclear shelter at Olajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm looking at my watch. Is it time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Normally it's at a quarter past, because we started at a quarter to. So we have one hour and a half. But if you would prefer to have it now, we could have it earlier if that suits you, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honours. I can proceed. It's not a problem. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In this group of which you were a member were there special groups laying mines in certain parts of the territory and how many such groups were there, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no people laying mines in my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In that army which was at Olajnica were there groups dealing with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no such groups in Olajnica. They were located somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know in the Vukovar Hospital area what parts were mined?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that any mines were laid around the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say in the hospital; I said around the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said. I don't know that any areas around the hospital were mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Up to the 20th of November, you say that you visited the Vukovar Hospital on numerous occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And you explained the reasons and everything else. What I would like to know is the following: When you were visiting the Vukovar Hospital, did you see any defence commanders, I'm referring specifically to Mr. Dedakovic, in the Vukovar Hospital, and did you see that he had any contacts with the people from the Vukovar Hospital? I'm referring to the staff here, the doctors and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Mr. Dedakovic inside the hospital on any of my visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Borkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain who he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Vukovar defence after Dedakovic, but I learned that only later. I never saw him in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Ivica Arbanas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I saw him on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain who this is and what he was doing in Vukovar? Describe the situations and places where you saw him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croatian soldier. I saw him at Olajnica. He would sometimes come there to rest, because it was relatively quiet there. So he would come there to rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Where did he rest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in a flat in a residential building at Olajnica, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that your commanding officer, whose name we will not mention, or any of those people maintained contacts with Vesna Bosanac or Dr. Njavro in the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was contact with Dr. Vesna Bosanac during the visits. When my group went to visit, there were oral contacts with Dr. Bosanac. We would report what we had brought, when we would bring something else, ask if the hospital needed anything else, and after unloading the food or the clothing we would leave. That is the contact I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this immediate contact was there any contact by telephone, radio or in any other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, not a single telephone in the town was functioning, and I'm not aware of any radio contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by the Canadians you said that you saw there was no other way out, that it was all over, and that you had to take the civilians to the hospital. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you let me look at the document and then I will be able to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Look at page 8 of your transcript. That's the transcript from that interview. The ERN number is 0059-6125.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. That's my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As this is a transcript, this is probably a verbatim transcript of what you said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know is the following. You say: "We had to transfer these civilians to the hospital." I want to know what "had to" means. Who was it who issued this decision? Who reached the conclusion that civilians had to be transferred and who issued the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the 18th, we came to understand that all resistance was over. I don't think the precise date is mentioned here. This decision was finally made when the woman in the white flag turned up who has been mentioned more than once, yesterday and today. And then it was said that civilians and whoever else wanted to go to Serbia should go to the piazza; those who didn't want to go to Serbia should go to the hospital. And then we transferred the civilians as I described. I helped the women, the children, the elderly, and I showed the way to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that. But what do you mean by "we had to," why this compulsiveness? What exactly was the reason that you had to? These civilians had in no way been involved in the fighting. What was the reason for so urgently taking them across to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This woman carrying a white flag came over, and she said it loud and clear, those who wanted to go towards the army should head for the square, and those who wanted to go back to Croatia were to go to the hospital. She appeared to be in possession of some sort of information. She looked quite dependable as she was saying this, and she was carrying a white flag. This was the morning of the 19th. We realised that all resistance was hopeless by this time and we just gave it up. Someone came along carrying a white flag, and we all know what a white flag normally means; it is a symbol of surrender. We heard what this lady had to say and we decided to follow suit, to try to get our civilians across to the hospital. That was our conclusion. That's my conclusion, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This was on the 19th of November, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the surrender of the Mitnica group on the 18th and about the civilians from Mitnica, what became of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know now, but I -- or we had no inkling at the time of their surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to your arrival at the hospital on the 19th, did you know about any attempts by the so-called Croatian army and the town's defenders to leave Vukovar, to escape from Vukovar and what became of those attempts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were attempts, but I didn't know at the time what, if anything, those attempts had come to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone offer you as a defender of Vukovar to leave Vukovar in this way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to leave with a group that included Marin Mercep. I was asleep, having stood guard for some time, that was two or three days previously, that was between the 15th and the 18th. I was asleep, and they simply failed to inform me that they would be off. They just left town, and I stayed behind. I later heard that there were other groups heading out, but I did not wish to join them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So the reason you didn't go was the fact that you happened to be asleep at the time, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may sound strange, but that is a fact. If you stand outside in the cold for 12 hours in a row, the next morning you're likely to be knackered, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So you wake up the next morning, you realise that your fellow fighters are gone, your commander is gone. As far as I understand, he is at the hospital by this time, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So what do you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. I was just there with those civilians. I do have to say that there were close contacts with those people -- or, rather, we were close by this time. We had been through a lot together. They trusted me. I was the one who brought them food. The children looked at me as though I was some sort of Santa Claus. I always had bubble-gums in my pockets to divvy out to these kids. We didn't do much, really. We just sat there. There was an air of uncertainty surrounding the whole situation, and we were afraid to even think of what would become of us. For the last two days, there were no operations going on. We used up whatever old stale bread we still had and some that we managed to bake ourselves. As for our water supplies, there was less than a glass -- a daily glass per person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I will have to interrupt you here. I'm just asking what you eventually did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me what I was doing, the he answer is nothing, nothing much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What time it was when you eventually reached the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sometime in the morning hours, but I can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How many civilians were in that group that came with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say several hundreds, between 600 and 700 civilians left. There were about 500 from the nuclear shelter. And perhaps another one or 200 joined on the way, people who were leaving the residential buildings. Across Olajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This was on the 19th in the morning hours. I just wish to have that confirmed because it's not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would this be a good time for our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It is, indeed, Mr. Bulatovic. We are going to have a break of a half hour because there is a need for a redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Your Honour leaves, if that's all right, with regard to the next witness Grujic, I've actually requested that he remain just in case it's feasible for that witness to be started. I have looked at my re-examination, and I believe it will be very short. So I don't know if that assists my learned friends in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you said one hour and a half, so perhaps we may be able to reach it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An hour, an hour and a quarter perhaps. I hope that I will be able to finish this witness and leave the rest to Mr. Moore. I don't think he will need so much time in re-examination, but -- I really don't know how we can do this. We should be done by 4.30. I only have 45 minutes. I really have no idea how Mr. Moore can re-examine this witness. I will try to wrap this up as fast as I possibly can. I will try to stick to my previous promise. I am not sure what the chances are though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on that, Mr. Bulatovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let us continue, sir. Were you asked by Mr. Vasic a question, and you said that you knew about some of those arriving in the hospital putting bandages on with no injuries or applying plaster-casts on different parts of their bodies and some of them were putting on white overcoats in order to pass themselves off as medical staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is how many of those who had bandages with no injuries. Can you tell us that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about two, three perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the number of people who had plaster-casts applied for no reason at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am referring to that whole group, plaster-casts and bandages, I would say is comprised two or three individuals whose names I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about the number of people who put on white overcoats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without being medical staff, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same figure; two or three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 19th there was an evacuation of civilians to the Velepromet facility. On the 19th during the evacuation, did you see Vesna Bosanac anywhere inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Dr. Juraj Njavro?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Zeljka Zgonjanin ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. It's not familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Zeljka, Zeljka, it's actually a lady.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a lady named Zeljka. I didn't know her surname. She was a member of the Vukovar Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely the person I'm talking about. I want to know whether she was involved in the evacuation on the 19th. Is this something you are aware of? I'm talking about the evacuation of civilians to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-030 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I got that. I'm just thinking. Not as far as I know, she wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: During your time at the hospital on the 19th, and the 20th, did you hear people talking about the civilians possibly being taken to Velepromet?
